newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong to appeal against US extradition decision.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong to appeal against US extradition decision.

text.p: Hong Kong is mounting an urgent appeal against a U.S. court's refusal to extradite a fugitive to the British colony because of its impending handover to China, Governor Chris Patten said on Wednesday.

The ruling by the court in Boston undermined Hong Kong's efforts to convince the world that it would retain its freedoms, particularly judicial independence, after it reverts to China at midnight on June 30, 1997.

U.S. District Judge Joseph Tauro ruled on Tuesday against extraditing Jerry Lui Kin-hong, a former commercial director of British-American Tobacco Co (Hong Kong) Ltd, to face multi-million dollar bribery and conspiracy charges relating to cigarette smuggling.

Tauro granted a writ of habeas corpus in response to defence arguments that Lui faced possible execution if forced to return to Hong Kong because his trial was unlikely to be completed before the handover to China.
"I have to say that we were literally amazed by the decision," Patten told a news conference. "We'll be urgently seeking an appeal and seeking to delay the release of the gentleman in question."
The United States and Hong Kong signed an agreement only last month preventing the surrender of fugitives to a third jurisdiction such as China, ensuring they remained in Hong Kong.

"The act reflects America's support for Hong Kong's high degree of autonomy, including the independence of the legal and judicial system, after the territory's reversion to China next July," U.S. Consul-General Richard Boucher said at the time.
Hong Kong formally abolished capital punishment only recently but no executions have been carried out in the British colony since November, 1966. Executions are common in China.
Lui, who became a Canadian citizen in 1994, will be released in 10 days from a state prison in Plymouth, Massachusetts, pending an appeal by the U.S. government, officials said.
He was arrested at Boston's Logan airport in December, 1995.

Hong Kong's Attorney-General would spare no efforts in fighting the decision which risks setting a precedent for others seeking to oppose extradition from the United States, a legal department spokesman said.
"We would point out that District Judge Tauro's decision flies in the face of a number of other recent extradition cases," he said.
"For example, in a recent extradition case, the Canadian courts rejected arguments similar to those put forward by Mr Lui.
"We will be stressing in the appeal that Hong Kong will continue to enjoy a legal system separate from that of China after 1 July, 1997."
According to the terms of the Sino-British Joint Declaration signed in 1984, Britain promised to end 150 years of colonial rule and cede its last Asian outpost to China.

Beijing in return promised to refrain from imposing Chinese socialism on the bustling capitalist community of 6.3 million people and permit Hong Kong people to maintain their legal and social systems.

"We think it's imperative that people recognise that under the Sino-British Joint Declaration...Hong Kong will be a separate jurisdiction in terms of the administration of justice from China," said Patten, who was speaking before departing later in the day for talks in London.
"That's embodied in an international treaty. And we don't think it should be questioned by anyone."
